claim: A two-color in vivo STED microscope was designed with ~8% crosstalk of EYFP in the EGFP channel and ~5% of the EGFP signal in the EYFP channel.
source: Live-cell imaging showed that we have designed a virtually crosstalk-free microscope with only ~8% crosstalk of EYFP in the EGFP channel (channel 1) and ~5% of the EGFP signal in the EYFP channel (channel 2) which does not require linear unmixing (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C demonstrating the crosstalk percentages.

claim: The two-color STED microscope achieves a resolution of at least ~70 nm for Citrine and ~84 nm for EGFP in vivo.
source: STED microscopy visualized dendrites, spines, and attached PSD95 assemblies in layer 1 of the visual cortex at superresolution (Figure 1C) with a resolution of at least ~70 nm for Citrine and ~84 nm for EGFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The resolution values are determined from experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Spine head area correlates with PSD95 area for both EE and control mice.
source: The spine head area correlated with the PSD95 area for EE and Ctr (Figure 2B), corroborating EM and two-photon microscopy studies (Arellano et al., 2007; Cane et al., 2014; Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: The correlation is demonstrated by data in Figure 2B and is consistent with previous studies cited.

claim: The median spine head area for EE housed mice is 0.527 µm² with an interquartile range of 0.359–0.844 µm².
source: We determined a median spine head area for EE housed mice of 0.527 (interquartile range [IR]: 0.359–0.844) µm2 and 0.462 (IR: 0.290–0.787) µm2 for Ctr mice.
evidence: The median and interquartile range values are derived from direct measurements of spine head areas.

claim: The median spine head area for control mice is 0.462 µm² with an interquartile range of 0.290–0.787 µm².
source: We determined a median spine head area for EE housed mice of 0.527 (interquartile range [IR]: 0.359–0.844) µm2 and 0.462 (IR: 0.290–0.787) µm2 for Ctr mice.
evidence: The median and interquartile range values are derived from direct measurements of spine head areas.

claim: The median PSD95 area for EE housed mice is 0.158 µm² with an interquartile range of 0.107–0.269 µm².
source: The area of PSD95 on the same set of spine heads was 0.158 (IR: 0.107–0.269) µm2 in median for EE mice and 0.161 (IR: 0.092–0.286) µm2 for Ctr mice which is in accordance with previous EM studies reporting 0.15 µm2 for the PSD area in the mouse visual cortex (Harris and Weinberg, 2012).
evidence: The median and interquartile range values are derived from direct measurements of PSD95 areas and are consistent with previous EM studies.

claim: The median PSD95 area for control mice is 0.161 µm² with an interquartile range of 0.092–0.286 µm².
source: The area of PSD95 on the same set of spine heads was 0.158 (IR: 0.107–0.269) µm2 in median for EE mice and 0.161 (IR: 0.092–0.286) µm2 for Ctr mice which is in accordance with previous EM studies reporting 0.15 µm2 for the PSD area in the mouse visual cortex (Harris and Weinberg, 2012).
evidence: The median and interquartile range values are derived from direct measurements of PSD95 areas and are consistent with previous EM studies.

claim: The distributions of spine head and PSD95 areas are significantly different between EE and control mice.
source: The histograms of spine head (Figure 2C) and PSD95 area (Figure 2D) were positively skewed and the distributions were significantly different between EE and Ctr mice.
evidence: Statistical analysis (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) of the data shown in Figure 2C and 2D demonstrates significant differences.

claim: Spine head and PSD95 area distributions are log-normally distributed.
source: All four histograms (Figure 2E and F) are symmetric and well described by a Gaussian function. This is in line with prior work showing that the spine and PSD95 fluorescence is log-normally distributed in general, which is predicted by multiplicative processes of ongoing spine plasticity (Hazan and Ziv, 2020; Loewenstein et al., 2011).
evidence: The log-transformed data shown in Figure 2E and F fit Gaussian distributions, consistent with log-normal distributions, and this is supported by previous studies.

claim: EE housed mice have significantly larger average spine head area compared to control mice.
source: The Gaussian function fitting the spine head area is shifted to the right and is narrower for EE housed mice (Figure 2E). This is manifested by a significantly larger spine head area (Figure 2G) and smaller variance of the size distribution (Figure 2I) of EE housed mice, which might imply a preferential loss or adaptation of small spines (Figure 2E).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G demonstrates significantly larger spine head area in EE mice (unpaired t-test with Welch's correction: p < 0.0001).

claim: EE housed mice have significantly smaller variance in spine head size distribution compared to control mice.
source: The Gaussian function fitting the spine head area is shifted to the right and is narrower for EE housed mice (Figure 2E). This is manifested by a significantly larger spine head area (Figure 2G) and smaller variance of the size distribution (Figure 2I) of EE housed mice, which might imply a preferential loss or adaptation of small spines (Figure 2E).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 2I demonstrates significantly smaller variance in EE mice (unpaired t-test with Welch's correction: p = 0.006).

claim: The average PSD95 area is not significantly different between EE and control mice.
source: The distributions of the logarithm of the PSD95 area (Figure 2F) are almost centered and thus the average area is not significantly different between EE and Ctr mice (Figure 2H).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 2H shows no significant difference (unpaired t-test with Welch's correction: p = 0.54).

claim: EE housed mice have significantly smaller variance in PSD95 area distribution compared to control mice.
source: However, the variance (Figure 2J) is smaller for EE housed mice which is also visible in the Gaussian distribution that is narrower for EE housed mice (Figure 2F), that is, having less extreme values.
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 2J demonstrates significantly smaller variance in EE mice (unpaired t-test with Welch's correction: p = 0.003).

claim: Spine density is not significantly different between EE and control housed mice.
source: We also analyzed the spine density which was not significantly different between EE and Ctr housed mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B demonstrates no significant difference (Mann-Whitney U test, p = 0.68).

claim: Spine heads grow by approximately 20% and shrink by approximately 15% within 30 minutes.
source: Interestingly, PSD95 assemblies displayed larger normalized changes in size than spine heads, which is evident from the elliptic distributions in Figure 3D–G or the median percent changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E); spine heads grew by ~20% and shrunk by ~15% while PSD95 assemblies grew by ~20–25% and shrunk by 25–30%.
evidence: The percentage changes are derived from measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PSD95 assemblies grow by approximately 20-25% and shrink by 25-30% within 30 minutes.
source: Interestingly, PSD95 assemblies displayed larger normalized changes in size than spine heads, which is evident from the elliptic distributions in Figure 3D–G or the median percent changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E); spine heads grew by ~20% and shrunk by ~15% while PSD95 assemblies grew by ~20–25% and shrunk by 25–30%.
evidence: The percentage changes are derived from measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Temporal changes between spine head and PSD95 area show weak but significant positive correlation (r between 0.15 and 0.39).
source: A linear regression analysis revealed a weak but significant positive correlation (r between 0.15 and 0.39, Figure 3D–G), such that an increase of PSD95 area is more frequently accompanied by an increase in spine head area and vice versa (Figure 3K).
evidence: Linear regression analysis of data shown in Figure 3D-G demonstrates weak positive correlations with statistical significance (p < 0.0001).

claim: The variance of positively correlated changes (PC1) is approximately 3 times larger than negatively correlated changes (PC2) at all time intervals.
source: The variance of PC1 and thus correlated changes is ~3 times larger at all time intervals than that of PC2, that is, anti-correlated changes (Figure 3H, I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Principal component analysis results shown in Figure 3H, I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F demonstrate the variance ratio.

claim: Control housed mice show statistically significantly higher variance for negatively correlated changes (PC2) compared to EE housed mice.
source: Thus, the variance of Ctr housed mice was statistically significantly higher for PC2 but not for PC1.
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 3J demonstrates significantly higher variance for PC2 in control mice (unpaired t-test: p < 0.0001).

claim: Negatively correlated changes contribute much less in EE housed mice, indicating stronger positive coupling between spine head size and PSD95 area changes.
source: This indicates that negatively correlated changes contribute much less in the EE housed mice indicating a stronger, positive coupling between changes in spine head size and PSD95 area.
evidence: This is inferred from the significantly lower variance of PC2 in EE mice shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Large spines tend to shrink and small spines tend to grow, exhibiting regression to the mean.
source: Plotting the size difference between the different time points as a function of the original size indicates that large spines tend to shrink and small spines tend to grow; this becomes evident as the changes are rather negative for larger sizes and positive for smaller sizes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Such a tendency is often called regression to the mean and is a frequently observed statistical phenomenon.
evidence: The tendency is demonstrated by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and is characterized as a known statistical phenomenon.

claim: The multiplicative downscaling factor for PSD95 area is significantly different between EE and control housed mice.
source: We observed a significantly different slope, that is, multiplicative downscaling for the PSD95 area between EE and Ctr housed mice (Figure 4F).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F demonstrates significantly different slopes between EE and control mice at 30, 60, and 120 min intervals (p < 0.01, p < 0.0001, p < 0.0001 respectively).

claim: The slope for spine head size changes is constant over time and similar between EE and control mice.
source: Interestingly, this effect was specific for PSD95 and was not observed for the spine head size (Figure 4A–C); the slope for spine head size changes was rather constant over time and similar between EE and Ctr mice.
evidence: Analysis shown in Figure 4A-C demonstrates no significant differences in slopes for spine head changes between EE and control mice.

claim: Large spine heads tend to stay rather large and smaller ones stay small over the 2-hour observation period.
source: The r value was relatively constant over all time intervals and not significantly different between spine heads and PSD95 assemblies or EE and Ctr house mice. As such we did not find changes in r or its corresponding coefficient of determination R2 value such as described in vitro (Hazan and Ziv, 2020) at our time window of up to 2 hr. This indicates that large spine heads tend to stay rather large and smaller ones stay small.
evidence: The stability is inferred from the constant Pearson's correlation coefficient r shown in Figure 4C and F over different time intervals.

claim: No temporal shift between spine head and PSD95 area changes was observed at baseline.
source: Figure 4G shows that the cross-correlation between the PSD95 and spine head area was ~0.8 over all time intervals of 0–120 min and thus we did not observe directional changes of these parameters at baseline. In particular, we did not observe that PSD95 increase would systematically succeed a spine head increase or vice versa as both would result in an asymmetric cross-correlation.
evidence: Cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4G demonstrates symmetric correlation without temporal lag.

claim: Control housed mice show a clear trend where the longer the measurement interval, the greater the morphological change in PSD95 nanoorganization.
source: Ctr housed mice showed a clear trend: the longer the measurement interval, the greater the morphological change (Figure 5C); the percentage of PSD95 nanoorganization showing no change decreased from ~40% to ~10%, while the percentage for strong changes nearly tripled for Ctr.
evidence: The trend is demonstrated by visual inspection data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For EE housed mice, approximately 20% of PSD95 assemblies did not change and approximately 80% underwent a change at all time points.
source: For EE housed mice, we observed similar, strong changes within all investigated time intervals; ~20% of the PSD95 assemblies did not change at all and ~80% underwent a change at all time points (Figure 5B).
evidence: The percentages are derived from visual inspection data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PSD95 nanoorganization is more dynamic in EE mice than in mice raised under control conditions within the investigated time course.
source: Thus, changes in Ctr housed mice increased over the observation period and reached a level similar to that of EE housed mice after 120 min. This suggests that the PSD95 nanoorganization is more dynamic in EE mice than in mice raised under control conditions within the investigated time course.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the comparison of morphological change patterns shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Fewer nanoorganizations of EE housed mice were perforated and a larger fraction showed three or more clusters compared to control mice.
source: Fewer nanoorganizations of EE housed mice were perforated and a larger fraction showed three or more clusters compared to Ctr mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: The morphometry differences are shown in Figure 5D based on visual categorization.

claim: Environmental enrichment accelerates the maturation of new neurons.
source: EE has been shown to accelerate the maturation of new neurons, increase pre- and post-synaptic protein levels (Nithianantharajah et al., 2004), and facilitate synaptic plasticity (Greifzu et al., 2014; Nithianantharajah and Hannan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Environmental enrichment increases pre- and post-synaptic protein levels.
source: EE has been shown to accelerate the maturation of new neurons, increase pre- and post-synaptic protein levels (Nithianantharajah et al., 2004), and facilitate synaptic plasticity (Greifzu et al., 2014; Nithianantharajah and Hannan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nithianantharajah et al., 2004.

claim: Environmental enrichment facilitates synaptic plasticity.
source: EE has been shown to accelerate the maturation of new neurons, increase pre- and post-synaptic protein levels (Nithianantharajah et al., 2004), and facilitate synaptic plasticity (Greifzu et al., 2014; Nithianantharajah and Hannan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Greifzu et al., 2014 and Nithianantharajah and Hannan, 2006.

claim: Environmental enrichment increases dendritic branching and spine density.
source: Structural changes include increased dendritic branching and spine density (Gelfo et al., 2009; Leggio et al., 2005) and induction of spine formation (Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gelfo et al., 2009 and Leggio et al., 2005.

claim: Environmental enrichment induces spine formation.
source: Structural changes include increased dendritic branching and spine density (Gelfo et al., 2009; Leggio et al., 2005) and induction of spine formation (Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2009.

claim: There is a tight correlation between structural plasticity and functional plasticity.
source: Decades of neuroscience research has shown a tight correlation between structural plasticity, the morphological transformation of spines and synapses, and modifications in synaptic transmission, termed functional plasticity (Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2001), which was confirmed recently at ultrastructural resolution (Holler et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2001 and Holler et al., 2021.

claim: Functional changes are linked to anchoring AMPAR via TARPs to PSD95.
source: Functional changes are linked to anchoring amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPAR) via transmembrane AMPAR-regulatory proteins (TARPs) to the post-synaptic density (PSD) scaffolding protein PSD95 (Compans et al., 2016; Herring and Nicoll, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Compans et al., 2016 and Herring and Nicoll, 2016.

claim: AMPAR-mediated currents increase simultaneously with the spine head directly after LTP induction.
source: AMPAR-mediated currents were shown to increase simultaneously with the spine head directly after LTP induction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge without specific citation in this sentence.

claim: Accumulations of PSD95 increase with a delay of approximately 1 hour after inducing LTP, whereas spine heads increase in less than a minute.
source: Recent evidence suggests that not all synaptic structures follow this fast dynamic; as such, accumulations of PSD95 increase in vitro with a delay of ~1 hr after inducing LTP, whereas the spine heads increase in less than a minute (Bosch et al., 2014; Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bosch et al., 2014 and Meyer et al., 2014.

claim: PSD95 is often arranged in clusters, rings, or a more complex nanopattern.
source: By applying superresolution microscopy we and others have shown that PSD95 is often arranged in clusters, rings, or a more complex nanopattern, and that this nanoorganization undergoes pronounced intrinsic structural changes on the time scale of minutes to hours (Hruska et al., 2018; MacGillavry et al., 2013; Wegner et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hruska et al., 2018, MacGillavry et al., 2013, and Wegner et al., 2018.

claim: PSD95 nanoorganization undergoes pronounced intrinsic structural changes on the time scale of minutes to hours.
source: By applying superresolution microscopy we and others have shown that PSD95 is often arranged in clusters, rings, or a more complex nanopattern, and that this nanoorganization undergoes pronounced intrinsic structural changes on the time scale of minutes to hours (Hruska et al., 2018; MacGillavry et al., 2013; Wegner et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hruska et al., 2018, MacGillavry et al., 2013, and Wegner et al., 2018.

claim: Sub-synaptic nanoorganization exists at the pre- and post-synaptic site and both are aligned in nanocolumns.
source: Recently, it was shown that such a sub-synaptic nanoorganization exists at the pre- and post-synaptic site and that both are aligned in the so-called nanocolumns (Hruska et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hruska et al., 2018 and Tang et al., 2016.

claim: Changes in the shape of the PSD or modest clustering of AMPAR is a highly efficient way to modify synaptic strength without altering the total amount of receptors.
source: Computational studies show that changes of the shape of the PSD (Franks et al., 2003) or modest clustering of AMPAR (Savtchenko and Rusakov, 2014) is a highly efficient way to modify synaptic strength without altering the total amount of receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational studies by Franks et al., 2003 and Savtchenko and Rusakov, 2014.

claim: AMPAR current amplitude drops significantly already at 50 nm offset between pre-synaptic glutamate release site and AMPAR cluster.
source: Moreover, AMPAR current amplitude drops significantly already at 50 nm offset between pre-synaptic glutamate release site and AMPAR cluster (Haas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haas et al., 2018.

claim: Synaptic connections undergo continuous spontaneous remodeling without any activity.
source: Synaptic structures, however, are highly volatile intrinsically as such that synaptic connections undergo continuous spontaneous remodeling without any activity (Mongillo et al., 2017; Ziv and Brenner, 2018); for example, intact synapses are formed despite abolishing pre-synaptic release (Sigler et al., 2017) or network silencing (Hazan and Ziv, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mongillo et al., 2017 and Ziv and Brenner, 2018.

claim: Intact synapses are formed despite abolishing pre-synaptic release.
source: Synaptic structures, however, are highly volatile intrinsically as such that synaptic connections undergo continuous spontaneous remodeling without any activity (Mongillo et al., 2017; Ziv and Brenner, 2018); for example, intact synapses are formed despite abolishing pre-synaptic release (Sigler et al., 2017) or network silencing (Hazan and Ziv, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sigler et al., 2017.

claim: Intact synapses are formed despite network silencing.
source: Synaptic structures, however, are highly volatile intrinsically as such that synaptic connections undergo continuous spontaneous remodeling without any activity (Mongillo et al., 2017; Ziv and Brenner, 2018); for example, intact synapses are formed despite abolishing pre-synaptic release (Sigler et al., 2017) or network silencing (Hazan and Ziv, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hazan and Ziv, 2020.

claim: The visual cortex exhibits enhanced plasticity under environmental enrichment conditions.
source: By investigating the synaptic dynamics in the mouse visual cortex, a brain region known to exhibit enhanced plasticity under EE conditions (Baroncelli et al., 2010; Kalogeraki et al., 2017) and accessible to light microscopy, we demonstrate that spine head and PSD95 size distributions decrease in variability while spine heads increase in average size under EE.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baroncelli et al., 2010 and Kalogeraki et al., 2017.

claim: PSD95.FingR efficiently labels endogenous PSD95.
source: We utilized a transcriptionally regulated antibody-like protein to visualize endogenous PSD95 without introducing overexpression artifacts (Gross et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gross et al., 2013.

claim: PSD95.FingR labeling excludes artifacts that occur after PSD95 overexpression.
source: We used the transcriptionally regulated antibody-like PSD95.FingR, which efficiently labels endogenous PSD95 (Cook et al., 2019; Gross et al., 2013) and excludes artifacts that occur after PSD95 overexpression (El-Husseini et al., 2000; Stein et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cook et al., 2019, Gross et al., 2013, El-Husseini et al., 2000, and Stein et al., 2003.

claim: The coefficient of determination R² between PSD95 brightness and nanoscale size is 0.76.
source: We also analyzed the PSD95 brightness and found a coefficient of determination R2 = 0.76 between the brightness and nanoscale size (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), indicating that the brightness is a deficient correlate of synaptic size.
evidence: The R² value is calculated from data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Brightness is a deficient correlate of synaptic size.
source: We also analyzed the PSD95 brightness and found a coefficient of determination R2 = 0.76 between the brightness and nanoscale size (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), indicating that the brightness is a deficient correlate of synaptic size.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the R² value of 0.76, which indicates substantial but imperfect correlation.

claim: The spine head growth of approximately 20-30% on average is very similar to spine head changes reported over 3-4 days in transgenic mice.
source: The spine head growth of ~20–30% on average and ~200% maximum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) is very similar to the spine head changes we have reported recently in the cortex of a transgenic mouse over 3–4 days (Steffens et al., 2021) and to spine head increase following chemical LTP induction (Kopec et al., 2006; Otmakhov et al., 2004) or glutamate uncaging (Meyer et al., 2014); thus these changes might reflect potentiation of single spines.
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to Steffens et al., 2021, Kopec et al., 2006, Otmakhov et al., 2004, and Meyer et al., 2014.

claim: MMF anesthesia reduces spiking activity and mildly increases spine turnover in the hippocampus.
source: However, it was shown that MMF anesthesia reduces spiking activity and mildly increases spine turnover in the hippocampus (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2021.

claim: The plasticity of spine heads and PSD95 assemblies might be different in the awake state and under intense processing of visual information.
source: Thus, the plasticity of spine heads and PSD95 assemblies might be different in the awake state and under intense processing of visual information.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the effects of anesthesia mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: In vitro LTP experiments show a temporal delay of approximately 60 minutes between spine and PSD95 increase.
source: This supports in vitro LTP experiments which have shown a temporal delay of ~60 min between spine and PSD95 increase (Bosch et al., 2014; Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bosch et al., 2014 and Meyer et al., 2014.

claim: Spine and PSD enlargement might be regulated by different pathways.
source: Although these experiments were performed in cell culture and with PSD95 overexpression, they indicate that spine and PSD enlargement might be regulated by different pathways (Compans et al., 2016; Herring and Nicoll, 2016).
evidence: This inference is supported by citations to Compans et al., 2016 and Herring and Nicoll, 2016.

claim: A slot model proposes that actin polymerization during LTP increases the number of slots which can harbor AMPA receptors.
source: A slot model proposes that the actin polymerization during LTP increases the number of slots which can harbor AMPA receptors (Herring and Nicoll, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Herring and Nicoll, 2016.

claim: In the slot model, the increase of AMPA receptors would not depend on an increase of the amount of PSD95 proteins at the synapse but on an activation of binding sites.
source: Thus, the increase of AMPA receptors would not depend on an increase of the amount of PSD95 proteins at the synapse but on an activation of binding sites of AMPA receptor to the PSD95 by a still unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference from the slot model described in the previous sentence.

claim: In the model of synaptic scaling, an increase in activity leads to a downscaling of excitatory synapses and vice versa.
source: In the model of synaptic scaling, an increase in activity leads to a downscaling of excitatory synapses and vice versa.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about synaptic scaling models.

claim: The downscaling in synaptic scaling is multiplicative and affects both the average and broadening of the size distribution.
source: The downscaling is multiplicative and therefore changes affect the average as well as broadening of the size distribution as shown, for example, in a silenced network (Hazan and Ziv, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hazan and Ziv, 2020.

claim: In the adult cortex, homeostatic plasticity is input-specific and not multiplicative for the whole ensemble of synapses.
source: This may be supported by recent in vivo observations that in the adult cortex homeostatic plasticity is rather input-specific and not multiplicative for the whole ensemble of synapses (Barnes et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Barnes et al., 2017.

claim: A decrease in variability of neuronal firing rates after stimulation implies that cortical circuits become more stable.
source: A sole decrease in variability was described before for the neuronal firing rates after stimulation. This was observed in different brain regions and even when the change in mean firing rate was little (Churchland et al., 2010). The authors of this study concluded that the variance decline of the firing rate implies that cortical circuits become more stable.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Churchland et al., 2010.

claim: The narrower size distributions in EE mice suggest that synapses are better defined by training in the enriched environment and the neural network is more stable.
source: The same might apply to the spines and synapses of EE housed mice for which we observe less extreme values. This may suggest that the synapses are better defined by training in the enriched environment and thus the neural network is more stable.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed narrower distributions and analogy to firing rate studies.

claim: Silencing a neuronal network results in an average size increase, broader distribution, and weaker multiplicative downscaling.
source: For example, it was shown that silencing a neuronal network and thus reducing its activity not only resulted in an average size increase and broader distribution but also in a weaker multiplicative downscaling (Hazan and Ziv, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hazan and Ziv, 2020.

claim: The increase in multiplicative downscaling observed in EE mice might explain the narrower size distribution of PSD95 area.
source: The increase in multiplicative downscaling we observe might explain the narrower size distribution of the PSD95 area according to the measurements and simulations by Hazan and Ziv, 2020.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on comparison with the work by Hazan and Ziv, 2020.

claim: PSDs on large spines are frequently perforated.
source: Previous EM studies have shown that PSDs on large spines, often called mushroom spines, are frequently perforated (Stewart et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stewart et al., 2005.

claim: Clusters of pre- and post-synaptic proteins are trans-synaptically aligned in nanocolumns which are organized by activity.
source: An emerging view is that clusters of pre- and post-synaptic proteins are trans-synaptically aligned in 'nanocolumns' which are organized by activity (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: A reorganization of receptors might alter synaptic strength independently of changes in the amount of receptors.
source: This implies that a reorganization of receptors might alter synaptic strength – independently of changes in the amount of receptors (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This inference is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: The increased structural plasticity of PSD95 nanoorganization but not increased average size in EE mice might reflect the reported increase of synaptic plasticity after enrichment.
source: Our finding of an increased structural plasticity of the PSD95 nanoorganization but not increased average size in EE mice might therefore reflect the reported increase of synaptic plasticity after enrichment (Artola et al., 2006; Buschler and Manahan-Vaughan, 2012).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to Artola et al., 2006 and Buschler and Manahan-Vaughan, 2012.

claim: Previous two-color STED microscopy of EGFP and EYFP suffered from high crosstalk requiring linear unmixing.
source: Previous attempts with STED microscopy of EGFP and EYFP utilized a single excitation wavelength and two-color detection, which suffered from high crosstalk, and therefore required a linear unmixing of the channels (Tønnesen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tønnesen et al., 2011.

claim: The most commonly used EGFP and EYFP have a crosstalk of as much as 92% and 27% in the respective other channel.
source: Thus, the most commonly used EGFP and EYFP have a crosstalk of as much as 92% and 27% in the respective other channel, requiring linear unmixing (Tønnesen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tønnesen et al., 2011.

claim: The PSD95 nanopattern labeled with PSD95.FingR is very similar to structures observed in a PSD95-EGFP knock-in mouse.
source: The pattern of the PSD95 nanoorganization labeled with PSD95.FingR was very similar to the structures we have observed earlier in a PSD95-EGFP knock-in mouse with in vivo STED microscopy (Wegner et al., 2018).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to Wegner et al., 2018.

claim: The PSD95 nanopattern is similar to perforated PSDs reported by electron microscopy.
source: And, this nanopattern is also similar to perforated PSDs reported by electron microscopy (Arellano et al., 2007; Harris and Weinberg, 2012; Toni et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arellano et al., 2007, Harris and Weinberg, 2012, and Toni et al., 2001.

claim: EE mice were housed in groups of up to 12 female mice.
source: EE mice were housed in a large, two-floor cage equipped with three running wheels for physical exercise, a labyrinth for cognitive stimulation, a tube and a ladder to change between the two levels, and were kept in groups of up to 12 female mice to allow manyfold social interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental housing conditions.

claim: Control mice were raised in pairs in standard cages without any equipment.
source: Ctr mice were raised in pairs in standard cages without any equipment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental housing conditions.

claim: Imaging commenced about 2.5 hours after onset of anesthesia.
source: Imaging commenced about 2.5 hr after onset of the anesthesia.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: The PSD95 area of layer 5 pyramidal neurons is slightly larger than previously reported diameter of 354 nm in a ubiquitously expressing PSD95-EGFP knock-in mouse.
source: This size of the PSD95 area of layer 5 pyramidal neurons is slightly larger than our previously reported diameter of 354 nm which corresponds to ~0.10 µm2 for a circular distribution, obtained in a ubiquitously expressing PSD95-EGFP knock-in mouse (Wegner et al., 2018); therefore, the larger size of the PSD95 area could reflect the larger size of the spine heads of layer 5 pyramidal neurons (Konur et al., 2003).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to Wegner et al., 2018 and Konur et al., 2003.

claim: The larger PSD95 area could reflect the larger size of spine heads of layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source: This size of the PSD95 area of layer 5 pyramidal neurons is slightly larger than our previously reported diameter of 354 nm which corresponds to ~0.10 µm2 for a circular distribution, obtained in a ubiquitously expressing PSD95-EGFP knock-in mouse (Wegner et al., 2018); therefore, the larger size of the PSD95 area could reflect the larger size of the spine heads of layer 5 pyramidal neurons (Konur et al., 2003).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to Konur et al., 2003.

claim: The average PSD area in the mouse visual cortex is 0.15 µm² according to EM studies.
source: The area of PSD95 on the same set of spine heads was 0.158 (IR: 0.107–0.269) µm2 in median for EE mice and 0.161 (IR: 0.092–0.286) µm2 for Ctr mice which is in accordance with previous EM studies reporting 0.15 µm2 for the PSD area in the mouse visual cortex (Harris and Weinberg, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harris and Weinberg, 2012.

claim: Spines were mostly stable over the time periods of 30, 60, and 120 minutes.
source: Over these time periods the spines were mostly stable.
evidence: This is an observation from the time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: Occasionally, a spine was lost or a new one appeared; none of these dynamic spines carried PSD95 and they were therefore most likely highly dynamic filopodia.
source: Occasionally, a spine was lost or a new one appeared; none of these dynamic spines carried PSD95 and they were therefore most likely highly dynamic filopodia (Berry and Nedivi, 2017).
evidence: This observation is supported by citation to Berry and Nedivi, 2017 for the characterization as filopodia.

claim: The average spine head area and PSD95 area did not show large changes over the time period of 120 minutes.
source: The average spine head area and PSD95 area did not show large changes over the time period of 120 min (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No directed changes were observed as a result of light-induced stimulation or phototoxicity.
